blocks.heading: What this section covers
blocks.text: Identify and compare the characteristic features of the source and of your own response; explain each difference by purpose, audience and context.

blocks.heading: What the comparison is
blocks.text: The comparison task sets your own Question 1(a) response beside the source, with the instruction Compare, and analyses form, structure and language. It is worth fifteen marks — five for reading, ten for analysis — and the analysis is of similarities and differences, each explained by the texts’ purposes, audiences and contexts. Two texts, one pair: the source that informed your response, and the response you wrote from it, which makes the comparison uniquely answerable — you know one of the texts because you made it.

blocks.heading: Planning the comparison
blocks.text: Planning a comparison starts from each text’s purpose, audience and form, and then matches features in pairs so each point holds both texts at once: the source’s headline beside the response’s salutation, both doing the job of first contact with their readers. The pairs are built on the three grounds the task names — form, structure, language — and a plan that lists one text’s features and then the other’s has not planned a comparison, only two descriptions.

blocks.heading: Connectives that carry the pair
blocks.text: Comparative connectives carry the pairing across both texts: whereas, similarly, in contrast, both, unlike. "Whereas the article opens with a headline that teases, my letter opens with a salutation that names its reader" holds both texts in one sentence. A sentence that uses none has described one text, not compared two, and the connectives are the visible machinery of the comparison — which is why they belong in every analytical paragraph, not only at the joins.

blocks.heading: Comparing what they say
blocks.text: The comparison is about how the two texts are written — form, structure and language — and not about what they say. "Both texts talk about the farm" compares content and earns little; "both texts open by promising the reader something — the article with a headline, my speech with a greeting — but the article teases while the speech assures" compares writing and earns it. The content matters as the thing carried, not the thing judged.

blocks.heading: Every difference has a reason
blocks.text: Each difference between the two texts has a reason, and the comparison names it: a different purpose, a different audience or a different context. A change of audience changes register — the same content for officials and for friends arrives in different vocabulary, contractions and sentence patterns — and the comparison shows the change at word level, quoting the Latinate verb from one and the contraction from the other. A named tone is a claim that must be proved by the words that create it: "urgent" is shown in the imperative verbs and short sentences, or it stays a guess the reader cannot check.

blocks.heading: Audience change at word level
blocks.text: The same bridge, for two readers. For the officials: “Inspection of the northern abutment revealed structural compromise requiring closure.” For the friends: “Honestly, the bridge is worse than we thought — they’ve shut it.” The officials’ version hides its agent in the passive and reaches for Latinate verbs, which suits a body that informs without alarming; the friends’ version contracts, intensifies and names nobody, because a friend wants the news rather than the procedure. A comparison that quotes these two side by side has already shown its reader the whole mechanism of audience: the difference is in every word, and the analysis only has to point.

blocks.heading: Forgetting half the pair
blocks.text: A comparison that writes mostly about the source and little about your own response abandons half its subject — and half the marks. The habit that cures it is the paired point: no paragraph stays on one text longer than a sentence before referring across. The reader should be able to cover either column of the answer and still find both texts in every paragraph, because the comparison is the relation, not the inventory.
